b1.keyPoint: Compton scatter involves loosely bound outer-shell electrons, depends on electron density not atomic number, and dominates in soft tissue at diagnostic and CT energies.

b2.keyPoint: Characteristic X-rays arise from electron transitions filling an inner-shell vacancy (created by electrons, photoelectric absorption or electron capture), never from nuclear gamma emission.

b3.keyPoint: Isotopes share proton number and chemical properties but differ in neutron number, mass number, binding energy and half-life.

b4.keyPoint: Increasing kVp raises tube output roughly with kVp squared, so skin and receptor dose rise, and the beam becomes harder and more penetrating.

b5.keyPoint: Breast compression reduces thickness and scatter, improving contrast and lowering mean glandular dose; magnification factors are always greater than 1.

b6.keyPoint: A smaller focal spot and reduced object-receptor distance both shrink penumbra, reducing geometric unsharpness and improving spatial resolution.

b7.keyPoint: In image-intensifier fluoroscopy the TV camera limits spatial resolution, electron lenses (not photomultipliers) do the focusing, and digital data undergo logarithmic conversion.

b8.keyPoint: DSA subtraction improves vessel contrast but combines noise from both frames, and cannot improve detector spatial resolution.

b9.keyPoint: CR plates use photostimulable barium fluorohalide (CsI is a DR material, NaI a gamma-camera material) and the latent image survives well beyond one hour.

b10.keyPoint: CT numbers express voxel attenuation relative to water in Hounsfield units; narrowing window width increases displayed contrast (lung window roughly WW 1500, WL -600 HU).

b11.keyPoint: CT dose is inversely related to pitch, whereas reconstructed slice thickness alone does not change patient dose.

b12.keyPoint: Increasing matrix size at fixed field of view makes pixels smaller, so fewer photons per pixel and lower CT SNR; larger pixels raise SNR.

b13.keyPoint: Thicker CT slices improve SNR; fat measures about -50 to -100 HU, air -1000 HU, and lung windows use a negative window level.

b14.keyPoint: The 0.5 mT static fringe field (not 0.5 T) defines the MRI controlled-access boundary, and many cochlear implants are MR conditional rather than contraindicated.

b15.keyPoint: In gamma cameras thallium activation boosts NaI light output, closer collimator-patient distance improves resolution, and thicker crystals raise sensitivity but degrade resolution.

b16.keyPoint: PET detects paired 511 keV annihilation photons in coincidence, achieving spatial resolution of roughly 4-8 mm.

b17.keyPoint: The ideal imaging radionuclide is a pure gamma emitter with a short physical half-life, since beta emission and long half-lives only add dose.

b18.keyPoint: SUV is a semi-quantitative FDG uptake index normalised to injected activity and body weight, varying with scanner and uptake time; the common malignancy threshold is about 2.5.

b19.keyPoint: SUV interpretation requires correction for the patient's blood glucose level before FDG injection.

b20.keyPoint: Internal radionuclide dose increases with longer physical (effective) half-life and slow organ clearance; scan duration does not change the committed dose.

b21.keyPoint: Mechanical index equals peak negative pressure divided by the square root of frequency, and indicates cavitation risk, significant above about 0.7 with microbubble contrast.

b22.keyPoint: Chemical shift artefact appears along the frequency-encoding direction, worsens at higher field strength, and is reduced by increasing receiver bandwidth, not by gadolinium.

b23.keyPoint: A long TE (about 120 ms) with long TR gives T2 weighting, and T1 is always longer than T2 in biological tissues.

b24.keyPoint: In gradient echo, shortening TE reduces susceptibility and metal artefact, while reducing flip angle lowers transverse magnetisation and hence SNR.

b25.keyPoint: SPECT improves contrast by tomographically separating overlying activity, but the rotating camera adds centre-of-rotation, motion and attenuation artefacts.

b26.keyPoint: PET is more sensitive than SPECT because it needs no physical collimator, and its radionuclides (C-11, N-13, O-15, F-18) have low atomic numbers.

b27.keyPoint: Spin echo uses a 90 degree excitation then a 180 degree refocusing pulse, which removes reversible dephasing so true T2* images cannot be produced.

b28.keyPoint: Under IRMER the employer establishes DRLs, practitioners need only be entitled and adequately trained (not necessarily doctors), and operators help keep doses ALARP.

b29.keyPoint: The IRMER practitioner justifies each medical exposure (the referrer only supplies clinical information), and practitioner and operator share optimisation duties.

b30.keyPoint: Deterministic effects have dose thresholds in the Gy range (lens opacity about 2 Gy); cancer is stochastic, and the lens is more radiosensitive than the cornea.

b31.keyPoint: Acoustic impedance equals density times sound speed (not frequency or attenuation), and a soft tissue-air interface reflects over 99% of the beam.

b32.keyPoint: Limit mechanical index to about 0.7 with microbubble contrast, and keep obstetric scanning below a thermal index of 3.0 with minimal exposure time.

b33.keyPoint: Sound speed depends on tissue stiffness and density, not frequency; wavelength equals speed divided by frequency, so it is proportional to speed.

b34.keyPoint: Doppler shift is proportional to transmitted frequency, blood velocity and the cosine of the angle - not to beam intensity or PRF.

b35.keyPoint: Pulsed Doppler aliases when the shift exceeds half the PRF (possible at physiological velocities), and aerated lung attenuates ultrasound at over 30 dB/cm/MHz.

b36.keyPoint: Short gamma-camera dead time permits dynamic studies, and breastfeeding interruption after Tc-99m depends on the specific radiopharmaceutical, not a universal 24 hours.

b37.keyPoint: Increasing pitch reduces CT dose - dose is inversely proportional to pitch when other factors are fixed.

b38.keyPoint: Chemical shift artefact is mapped along the frequency-encoding direction because fat and water resonate at slightly different frequencies.

b39.keyPoint: Classic chemical shift displacement occurs in the frequency-encoding direction, not the phase-encoding direction.

b40.keyPoint: Chemical shift artefact increases with field strength because the absolute fat-water frequency separation grows with B0.

b41.keyPoint: Increasing receiver bandwidth reduces chemical shift pixel displacement, at the cost of lower SNR.

b42.keyPoint: Gadolinium shortens T1 but has no effect on the fat-water frequency difference, so it does not alter chemical shift artefact.

b43.keyPoint: Titanium is non-ferromagnetic, so titanium implants do not align with or experience strong force from the static magnetic field.

b44.keyPoint: Ferromagnetic (ferrous) materials experience strong force and torque and align with the static magnetic field - the basis of MRI projectile risk.

b45.keyPoint: Decreasing window width increases displayed contrast by mapping a smaller HU range across the full greyscale.

b46.keyPoint: The absolute probability of Compton interaction falls slowly with increasing photon energy, so it is less likely at 120 kVp than 80 kVp.

b47.keyPoint: Compton scatter is the predominant photon interaction in soft tissue at diagnostic X-ray energies.

b48.keyPoint: Compton scatter requires photon energy well above the electron binding energy - it involves loosely bound outer-shell electrons.

b49.keyPoint: Compton interaction probability is proportional to tissue electron density, not atomic number.

b50.keyPoint: The scattered photon's residual energy falls as scatter angle increases, so mean energy at 90 degrees is lower than at 45 degrees.

b51.keyPoint: Compton interactions contribute to absorbed dose because the recoil electrons deposit energy locally in tissue.

b52.keyPoint: Water is defined as 0 HU on the Hounsfield scale; air is about -1000 HU and dense bone strongly positive.

b53.keyPoint: Beam hardening removes low-energy photons, lowering measured CT numbers and causing cupping artefact centrally.

b54.keyPoint: Entrance surface dose at a CT entry point exceeds that of most plain radiographs, though CT dose is distributed circumferentially.

b55.keyPoint: CT irradiates from many angles, giving a more uniform circumferential dose distribution than a single-projection radiograph.

b56.keyPoint: Effective dose is calculated from organ equivalent doses and tissue weighting factors - it is never assigned to a gram of tissue.

b57.keyPoint: Controlled areas are designated from likely exposure conditions and special procedure requirements, not from an examination exceeding 1 mSv effective dose.

b58.keyPoint: A 3 mSv effective dose threshold does not define a controlled area - designation depends on exposure conditions and regulatory criteria.

b59.keyPoint: Classified worker dose records are kept until age 75 or at least 30 years after work ceases, not until death.

b60.keyPoint: A typical adult non-contrast CT head effective dose is of the order of 1-3 mSv.

b61.keyPoint: Pre-patient collimation in CT primarily defines beam width and slice profile - it is not primarily a scatter-removal device.

b62.keyPoint: The gamma camera collimator provides spatial localisation by accepting only near-parallel photons; scatter rejection is done by energy windowing.

b63.keyPoint: An abdominal CT effective dose is of the order of 5-10 mSv, with protocol and patient variation.

b64.keyPoint: Effective dose in nuclear medicine depends on the radionuclide's biodistribution and residence time, which set the organ absorbed doses.

b65.keyPoint: BGO is used in PET for its high density and stopping power at 511 keV, not because its decay time beats NaI.

b66.keyPoint: Doppler shift is proportional to the cosine of the insonation angle, not to the raw angle itself.

b67.keyPoint: Doppler shift is directly proportional to the transmitted ultrasound frequency.

b68.keyPoint: Doppler shift is directly proportional to blood (reflector) velocity.

b69.keyPoint: Doppler shift depends only on transmitted frequency, reflector velocity and cosine of the angle - not reflector size.

b70.keyPoint: The Doppler equation contains only transmitted frequency, reflector velocity, cosine of angle and sound speed - nothing else changes the shift.

b71.keyPoint: Compton scatter can occur through angles up to 180 degrees, including full backscatter.

b72.keyPoint: F-18 has a physical half-life of approximately 110 minutes.

b73.keyPoint: The MR Safety Expert providing technical MR safety advice is usually a medical physicist.

b74.keyPoint: The MRI controlled area relates to the 0.5 mT fringe field contour, not 50 mT.

b75.keyPoint: The Faraday cage blocks external RF interference from corrupting the MR signal; it does not reduce the MRI signal or fringe field.

b76.keyPoint: Mo-99 (not Mo-68) is the parent isotope of Tc-99m in the generator.

b77.keyPoint: Tc-99m is eluted from a Mo-99/Tc-99m generator, not produced in a cyclotron (F-18 and I-123 are cyclotron products).

b78.keyPoint: Tc-99m emits a 140 keV (0.14 MeV) gamma photon.

b79.keyPoint: Tc-99m decays to Tc-99, whose half-life is so long it behaves as effectively stable for the patient.

b80.keyPoint: Tc-99m decays by isomeric transition, releasing its excess nuclear energy as gamma emission.

b81.keyPoint: SAR rises approximately with the square of the flip angle, since larger RF pulses deposit more energy.

b82.keyPoint: Detector element size and sampling pitch limit spatial resolution, alongside focal spot, motion and reconstruction factors.

b83.keyPoint: Adjacent detector rows can be combined, so a reconstructed CT slice can be wider than a single detector row.

b84.keyPoint: Soft-tissue ultrasound attenuation is roughly 0.5-1 dB/cm/MHz, far below 15 dB/cm/MHz.

b85.keyPoint: A larger acoustic impedance mismatch between tissues reflects a larger fraction of the ultrasound beam.

b86.keyPoint: Sound travels much faster in bone than in muscle or other soft tissue.

b87.keyPoint: Sound travels faster in muscle than in fat because muscle is stiffer.

b88.keyPoint: Sound speed in muscle is approximately 1540 m/s, the standard soft-tissue average used by scanners.

b89.keyPoint: Mechanical index indicates the risk of cavitation, important above about 0.7 with microbubble contrast.

b90.keyPoint: Thermal index estimates tissue temperature rise and is separate from mechanical index, which addresses cavitation.

b91.keyPoint: Mechanical index guides the operator on non-thermal (cavitation) risk, supporting keeping output as low as reasonably achievable.

b92.keyPoint: Mechanical index equals peak negative pressure divided by the square root of frequency, so it is inversely proportional to root frequency.

b93.keyPoint: Added filtration removes low-energy photons, so overall beam intensity leaving the tube decreases.

b94.keyPoint: Filtration reduces entrance skin dose by removing low-energy photons that would be absorbed superficially without contributing to the image.

b95.keyPoint: Filtration hardens the beam and usually reduces subject contrast, even though it lowers skin dose.

b96.keyPoint: Minimum total filtration for a standard diagnostic tube is typically 2.5 mm aluminium equivalent - 0.5 mm is insufficient.

b97.keyPoint: Beryllium tube windows are used below about 50 kVp (mammography) because they barely absorb the low-energy photons needed for breast contrast.

b98.keyPoint: Filtration modifies beam quality and patient dose; it is not used to limit a digital detector's dynamic range.

b99.keyPoint: CR plates are photostimulable barium fluorohalide; caesium iodide is a DR detector material.

b100.keyPoint: Doubling matrix dimensions from 512x512 to 1024x1024 quadruples pixel count and storage, it does not merely double them.

b101.keyPoint: A CR plate is a continuous phosphor - pixels are only created by sampling during laser readout.

b102.keyPoint: Positron annihilation occurs outside the nucleus, when the emitted positron meets an electron after travelling a short range in tissue.

b103.keyPoint: PET uses electronic coincidence detection of paired 511 keV photons and needs no physical parallel-hole collimator.

b104.keyPoint: A nominal fatal cancer risk of about 1 in 20,000 per mSv effective dose is the standard adult figure in radiological protection.

b105.keyPoint: Hereditary risk per mSv is far lower than 1 in 10,000 - the standard nominal figure is the 1-in-20,000 fatal cancer risk.

b106.keyPoint: The nominal fatal cancer risk is about 1 in 20,000 per mSv, not 1 in 300.

b107.keyPoint: SAR is proportional to the square of the Larmor frequency (and hence B0) and the square of the flip angle.

b108.keyPoint: Susceptibility artefact worsens with increasing static field strength.

b109.keyPoint: Susceptibility artefact causes signal loss, blooming and distortion, not simple brightening of the image.

b110.keyPoint: CR still uses automatic exposure control despite its wide dynamic range, to keep patient dose and noise appropriate.

b111.keyPoint: Tissue perfusion affects heating and thermal index interpretation; mechanical index addresses cavitation, not perfusion.

b112.keyPoint: Duplex ultrasound combines B-mode imaging with Doppler, not M-mode.

b113.keyPoint: Conventional spin echo begins with a 90 degree RF excitation pulse.

b114.keyPoint: The 180 degree refocusing pulse in spin echo reverses static dephasing and forms the echo.

b115.keyPoint: Spin echo gives true T2 weighting because the 180 degree pulse refocuses field inhomogeneity; T2* effects belong to gradient echo.

b116.keyPoint: More phase-encoding steps lengthen scan time and enlarge the phase matrix, but they do not require a longer TE.

b117.keyPoint: Air couples ultrasound very poorly - over 99% is reflected at a probe-air interface, which is why coupling gel is essential.

b118.keyPoint: A transducer heats more in air than on tissue because little acoustic energy is coupled away and internal losses stay in the probe.

b119.keyPoint: The Nyquist limit equals half the PRF, so increasing PRF raises the maximum Doppler shift measurable without aliasing.

b120.keyPoint: Diagnostic ultrasound wavelengths in soft tissue are approximately 0.1-1.5 mm across typical frequencies.

b121.keyPoint: Gradient echo lacks a 180 degree refocusing pulse, so susceptibility and field inhomogeneity cause more artefact than in spin echo.

b122.keyPoint: A single gamma camera crystal is viewed by an array of photomultiplier tubes whose relative signals localise each scintillation event.

b123.keyPoint: TR, the interval between successive excitations, is normally longer than TE, the time from excitation to echo.

b124.keyPoint: Diagnostic ultrasound uses roughly 2-15 MHz, with higher frequencies reserved for superficial structures.

b125.keyPoint: CR plates are read by laser stimulation, which releases the stored latent image as light for photomultiplier detection.

b126.keyPoint: SUV can help distinguish benign from malignant lesions (threshold about 2.5), though it is semi-quantitative and not definitive alone.

b127.keyPoint: A bow-tie filter shapes beam intensity to patient cross-section, reducing peripheral dose and equalising signal at the detector.

b128.keyPoint: Beta emission adds patient dose without contributing to imaging, which is why pure gamma emitters are preferred.

b129.keyPoint: The linear attenuation coefficient depends on composition, density, atomic number and photon energy - not the total mass of the object.

b130.keyPoint: DSA subtraction reduces SNR because noise variance from the mask and live images combines.

b131.keyPoint: A subtracted DSA image has better contrast conspicuity but no better spatial resolution than the unsubtracted images.

b132.keyPoint: Quantum mottle increases in a subtracted image because noise from both the mask and live frames adds.

b133.keyPoint: Iterative reconstruction permits lower-dose CT acquisition while maintaining diagnostic image quality.

b134.keyPoint: DSA delivers higher dose than standard fluoroscopy because it adds multiple high-dose acquisition runs.

b135.keyPoint: Aliasing occurs when the Doppler shift exceeds the Nyquist limit (half the PRF), which physiological blood velocities can exceed.

b136.keyPoint: Reducing object-to-detector distance reduces magnification and penumbra, decreasing geometric unsharpness.

b137.keyPoint: A smaller focal spot reduces penumbra and improves geometric sharpness.

b138.keyPoint: Geometric unsharpness is blur caused by focal spot size and imaging geometry - it is not a tool for excluding peripheral anatomy.

b139.keyPoint: Tomosynthesis improves depth separation and reduces tissue overlap, but in-plane spatial resolution is not necessarily better than 2D radiography.

b140.keyPoint: Tomosynthesis reconstructs multiple low-dose projections into a quasi-3D stack of slices.

b141.keyPoint: Tomosynthesis separates structures by depth, distinguishing overlying from underlying anatomy.

b142.keyPoint: Increasing a conductor's cross-sectional area lowers its resistance, so current rises for a fixed voltage.

b143.keyPoint: A longer effective half-life means more nuclear transformations occur in the patient, increasing absorbed dose.

b144.keyPoint: 1 cGy cm2 equals 1 uGy m2, because 1 cGy is 10,000 uGy and 1 m2 is 10,000 cm2.

b145.keyPoint: Barium enema DAP is quoted in Gy cm2 (about 45-50 Gy cm2) - dose-area product is dose multiplied by irradiated area, never plain Gy.

b146.keyPoint: A gamma camera processes successive scintillation events, acquiring many events during an examination, limited at high rates by dead time.

b147.keyPoint: Pitch is table advance per rotation divided by total beam collimation; dose is inversely related to pitch.

b148.keyPoint: Increasing pitch shortens scan time (and reduces dose) for a given coverage.

b149.keyPoint: CT colonography commonly uses 120 kVp, though low-dose protocols may use lower tube potentials.

b150.keyPoint: Extracellular gadolinium contrast has an elimination half-life of about 1.5 hours with normal renal function, not 2 minutes.

b151.keyPoint: Thermal index estimates tissue temperature rise and is affected by tissue attenuation, especially near bone.

b152.keyPoint: Iodinated CT contrast saturates thyroid iodine handling and reduces subsequent I-123 uptake, so study timing matters.

b153.keyPoint: Thermal index assumes average tissue conditions, so in highly perfused tissue it does not reflect true heating because blood flow carries heat away.

b154.keyPoint: Thermal index is high when scanning over superficial bone because bone strongly absorbs ultrasound and heats readily.

b155.keyPoint: CT artefacts increase at bone edges because abrupt attenuation transitions cause beam hardening, partial volume and streak artefacts.

b156.keyPoint: Ultrasound attenuation, and therefore heating and thermal index, increases with frequency - even over bone TI remains frequency dependent.

b157.keyPoint: A bone-muscle interface has a much larger acoustic impedance mismatch than muscle-fluid, so it reflects far more of the beam.

b158.keyPoint: SAR is reduced by lowering flip angle, using fewer RF pulses and lengthening TR - anything reducing deposited RF energy.

b159.keyPoint: Slice thickness is not a primary determinant of SAR, which depends on RF energy deposition.

b160.keyPoint: Field of view is not a primary determinant of SAR, which depends on RF energy deposition.

b161.keyPoint: Increasing TR allows more longitudinal magnetisation recovery, increasing signal and reducing SAR per unit time, at the cost of scan time.

b162.keyPoint: More phase-encoding (gradient) steps increase matrix size and scan time but do not by themselves improve SNR.

b163.keyPoint: Increasing B0 generally increases MR signal and SNR, though susceptibility artefact and SAR also increase.

b164.keyPoint: MRI SNR rises with the square root of the number of signal averages and with higher field strength.

b165.keyPoint: kVp changes beam energy and output but not focal spot size, which is set by filament, focusing cup and anode angle geometry.

b166.keyPoint: Bore width alone does not determine CT dose - protocol, filtration, tube current modulation and patient centring do.

b167.keyPoint: Iodine and gadolinium are positive contrast via high atomic number; air is negative contrast via very low density, not high Z.

b168.keyPoint: I-123 beats I-125 for imaging because its 159 keV photon suits the gamma camera and its shorter half-life lowers dose - chemistry is identical.

b169.keyPoint: Lowering kV reduces beam output and penetration, increases subject contrast, and reduces scatter production.

b171.keyPoint: At fixed mAs, lower kVp reduces photon output and penetration, so receptor dose falls.

b172.keyPoint: Decreasing kVp reduces Compton scatter production; scatter fraction rises with increasing kVp.

b173.keyPoint: Lower kVp means less scatter reaching the receptor; higher kVp increases the scatter fraction.

b174.keyPoint: Lowering kVp increases subject contrast because photoelectric absorption contributes relatively more at lower photon energies.

b175.keyPoint: PET/CT acquires the CT and PET datasets sequentially in the same examination, then fuses them.

b176.keyPoint: CT spatial resolution is far below 15 lp/mm - that figure belongs to mammography; CT achieves roughly 1 lp/mm or slightly more.

b177.keyPoint: Ultrasound contrast microbubbles are only a few micrometres across - far smaller than the wavelength and unrelated to probe dimensions.

b178.keyPoint: ESD is the entrance surface dose at the skin; the quantity incorporating irradiated area is dose-area product.

b179.keyPoint: Filtration reduces intensity and skin dose while raising mean beam energy and HVL - it removes photons, it does not add them.

b180.keyPoint: The X-ray tube is evacuated, tube current (not filament area) sets X-ray quantity, and anode heat is dissipated mainly by radiation.

b181.keyPoint: High kV increases beam intensity roughly with kVp squared but lowers subject contrast as Compton interactions dominate.

b182.keyPoint: Compression reduces tissue thickness and therefore scatter, improving contrast.

b183.keyPoint: CR phosphor layer thickness and crystal properties determine X-ray absorption, sensitivity and spatial resolution.

b184.keyPoint: CT typically uses a 512x512 matrix, bow-tie filtration, and shows cupping (low central HU) from beam hardening; the FBP filter is mathematical.

b185.keyPoint: Water is 0 HU, narrowing window width raises displayed contrast, metal causes photon starvation streaks, and multislice CT can still show ring artefact.

b186.keyPoint: Air is about -1000 HU, and isotropic voxels allow oblique multiplanar reconstruction with little loss of quality.

b187.keyPoint: Vignetting makes the image intensifier periphery dimmer than the centre, not brighter.

b188.keyPoint: Barium enema DAP is around 45-50 Gy cm2 and CT head effective dose 1-3 mSv; DAP conversions need both dose prefix and area handled together.

b189.keyPoint: Under IRMER the practitioner (not the referrer) justifies the exposure, the operator optimises it, and practitioners need not be doctors or dentists.

b190.keyPoint: The employer establishes local rules (with RPA advice) and ensures staff compliance; entering a controlled area does not automatically classify a worker.

b191.keyPoint: Clinical gamma camera resolution is about 10 mm (3 mm objects are not resolved), and the collimator localises photons - energy windowing rejects scatter.

b192.keyPoint: SPECT gives higher contrast, dose and attenuation-correction capability than planar imaging, but not better spatial resolution.

b193.keyPoint: PET needs no collimator, annihilation occurs outside the nucleus, and the coincidence timing window relates to detector separation and the speed of light.

b194.keyPoint: The ideal radiopharmaceutical has high chemical purity, gamma emission around 100-250 keV, no beta particles, and a half-life just long enough for imaging.

b195.keyPoint: Acoustic impedance is proportional to density; an air-tissue interface reflects about 99% while soft tissue-fluid interfaces reflect far below 15%.

b196.keyPoint: Doppler is a frequency (not velocity) change on reflection, maximal with the beam parallel to flow, and increased when blood moves towards the probe.

b197.keyPoint: T2* imaging exploits susceptibility dephasing, GRE shows flow as bright, and chemical shift displacement occurs along the frequency-encoding direction.

b198.keyPoint: MRI SNR increases with voxel size and TR, but falls with larger matrix, wider receiver bandwidth and longer TE.

b199.keyPoint: STIR suppresses all short-T1 tissue including gadolinium enhancement, so frequency-selective fat suppression is preferred after contrast.

b200.keyPoint: In- and opposed-phase imaging exploits the cyclical fat-water phase difference and detects microscopic fat by signal drop on opposed-phase images.

b201.keyPoint: MR Safe means no known hazard in any MR environment; demonstrated safety within defined conditions defines MR Conditional.

b202.keyPoint: SAR rises approximately with the square of flip angle; slice thickness and field of view are not primary SAR determinants.

b203.keyPoint: Microbubbles are a few micrometres across (much smaller than the wavelength); lead shields via high atomic number; low-eGFR gadolinium use is cautioned, not absolutely banned.

b204.keyPoint: For the same photon fluence, 1 g of bone absorbs more dose than 1 g of soft tissue because photoelectric absorption is greater in bone.

b206.keyPoint: Local ultrasound heating depends on the tissue absorption coefficient, blood perfusion and heat conduction away from the exposed region.

b207.keyPoint: Helium cryogen is inert (hazards are cold, pressure and asphyxiation on quench); the always-on static magnet is the biggest hazard, with 0.5 mT bounding the controlled area.

b208.keyPoint: Spin echo uses 90 and 180 degree pulses, cannot show T2* effects, and more phase-encoding steps do not improve signal via longer TE.

b209.keyPoint: Scatter can reach around 10 times the transmitted primary beam in large-field examinations.

b211.keyPoint: Doppler shift depends on transmitted frequency, reflector velocity, insonation angle and sound speed - not tissue density or compressibility.

b212.keyPoint: Sound speed varies with tissue temperature, and scanners assume an average soft-tissue speed of 1540 m/s, not 1240 m/s.

b213.keyPoint: Justification authority depends on employer entitlement and adequate training - there is no 5 mSv threshold reserving justification to radiologists.

b214.keyPoint: Radioactive gases and patient excreta count as radioactive waste, regulated by the environmental regulator rather than local councils.

b215.keyPoint: Effective focal spot size depends on target (anode) angle, filament size and focusing, and increases with mA through blooming.

b216.keyPoint: Grids improve contrast by absorbing scatter - they do not improve spatial resolution.

b218.keyPoint: DSA subtraction decreases SNR because mask and live image noise combine.

b219.keyPoint: Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) improves ultrasound axial resolution; TGC and monitor brightness change display only, not intrinsic resolution.

b223.keyPoint: Film badges measure beta, X and gamma radiation, TLD rings monitor finger dose, and electronic dosimeters are sensitive enough for real-time interventional monitoring.

b224.keyPoint: Effective dose requires tissue weighting factors and equals the uniform whole-body equivalent dose carrying the same stochastic risk.

b225.keyPoint: Compton probability tracks electron density, which differs between tissues, so the effect is not identical across all tissues at diagnostic energies.

b226.keyPoint: CR plates fade with time so should be read promptly, have lower limiting resolution than film, and their life is limited by handling not radiation heat.

b227.keyPoint: Flat panel detectors show far less geometric (pincushion, magnetic) distortion than image intensifiers.

b228.keyPoint: Beam hardening lowers central CT numbers (cupping), water is 0 HU, and ring artefact from faulty detector elements still occurs in multislice CT.

b229.keyPoint: Increasing pitch decreases CT dose, and cone beam artefact is worst away from the central plane where the beam is most oblique.

b230.keyPoint: After written declaration of pregnancy the fetal dose must be unlikely to exceed 1 mSv for the remainder; the employer reviews the risk assessment, and fluoroscopy is not automatically barred.

b231.keyPoint: CT uses 0.5-1 mm focal spots, solid-state detectors with 80-90% detection efficiency and low afterglow, filtered backprojection, and about 400 kB per 512x512 12-bit image.

b232.keyPoint: Quantum mottle worsens in obese patients, rib beam-hardening can mimic liver lesions, post-patient collimation reduces scatter, and pitch is dimensionless.

b237.keyPoint: Photoelectric absorption involves bound electrons and yields characteristic radiation, but Compton scatter is the main soft-tissue interaction at diagnostic energies.

b238.keyPoint: Sound speed equals 1 over the square root of (compressibility times density); it is highest in bone, and higher frequency improves resolution but cuts penetration.

b239.keyPoint: Reflection depends on acoustic impedance mismatch (not density alone), lung attenuates strongly, and lateral resolution is best on the central beam axis at focus.

b241.keyPoint: Apparent contrast rises with narrower window width, falls with higher kV and bright ambient lighting, and the eye distinguishes only about 256 grey levels.

b246.keyPoint: Gadolinium mainly shortens T1, has a plasma half-life of about 1.5 hours, and at eGFR below 30 is used with caution rather than absolutely contraindicated.

b247.keyPoint: I-123 is cyclotron-produced with a 13-hour half-life; field inhomogeneity affects T2* more than true T2.

b248.keyPoint: Tc-99m's 140 keV photons suit a low-energy gamma camera collimator.

b249.keyPoint: Compton scatter dominates diagnostic imaging but its absolute probability is slightly lower at 120 keV than at 80 keV.

b250.keyPoint: At constant receptor dose, higher kVp lets mAs fall so entrance skin dose decreases, while contrast falls and relative scatter increases.

b251.keyPoint: Increasing kVp raises mean beam energy, so the half-value layer increases.

b252.keyPoint: Grid ratio is strip height over interspace width (typically about 10:1), and the Bucky factor is the exposure increase a grid demands.

b253.keyPoint: With mAs fixed, raising kVp increases output and ESD roughly with kVp squared, increases scatter reaching the receptor, but leaves geometric unsharpness unchanged.

b254.keyPoint: Raising kVp hardens the beam, so the half-value layer increases.

b255.keyPoint: Mammography uses Mo/Mo target-filter, sub-millimetre focal spots, compression to cut dose, and an air gap instead of a grid in magnification views.

b256.keyPoint: MTF measures how contrast transfers across spatial frequencies - the standard resolution metric - and is degraded by scatter and motion blur.

b257.keyPoint: A typical image intensifier has a 25 cm CsI input phosphor, 2.5 cm output phosphor and 20-30 kV accelerating potential, giving minification gain.

b258.keyPoint: Reportable accidental exposures scale with intent: below 0.3 mSv intended, 3 mSv or more; 0.3-2.5 mSv, 10 times intended; 2.5-10 mSv, 25 mSv; above 10 mSv, 2.5 times intended.

b259.keyPoint: DSA uses logarithmic subtraction at around 70 kVp to enhance iodine conspicuity, improving low-contrast vessel perception but increasing noise.

b260.keyPoint: Nominal fatal cancer risk is about 1 in 20,000 per mSv for adults; excess childhood cancer risk is roughly 1 in 13,000 per mSv.

b261.keyPoint: Solid radioactive waste decays in shielded stores before disposal, and patient excreta are the main liquid waste source (about 40% for Tc-99m, 20% for FDG).

b262.keyPoint: Key half-lives: Tc-99m 6 hours, Mo-99 66 hours, F-18 110 minutes, I-123 13 hours.

b263.keyPoint: F-18 is cyclotron-produced, Tc-99m (not molybdenum) comes from the generator, and the gyromagnetic ratio is nucleus-specific, not tissue-specific.

b264.keyPoint: Susceptibility artefact worsens with increasing field strength and causes signal loss and blooming, not brightening.

b265.keyPoint: Compton scatter involves loosely bound electrons and depends on electron density; backscattered photons retain relatively low energy.

b266.keyPoint: Photoelectric absorption chiefly involves inner (K) shell electrons and scales with atomic number cubed, not with electron density.

b267.keyPoint: CR has wider dynamic range than film-screen; plate replacement follows wear and QA findings, not a fixed 3-year cycle.

b268.keyPoint: Mammography: Mo/Mo target-filter, useful spectrum near 20 keV, resolution about 15 lp/mm, mean glandular dose about 2 mGy, focal spot under 0.5 mm.

b269.keyPoint: Full-field digital mammography uses flat-panel digital detectors, not single-sided film-screen emulsion.

b270.keyPoint: Grids improve contrast at the cost of higher patient dose, so they are avoided for extremities and most paediatric patients.

b271.keyPoint: A grid controls scatter at the receptor - it does not reduce staff dose, which is managed by distance, shielding and collimation.

b272.keyPoint: Iterative reconstruction enables lower-dose CT; display FOV, reconstructed slice thickness and helical mode do not themselves cut dose, and higher pitch lowers it.

b273.keyPoint: Larger matrices need more storage, and film-screen can exceed many digital detectors in intrinsic spatial resolution.

b274.keyPoint: Effective dose can be estimated from DAP, the AP chest conversion factor exceeds PA, and local DRLs are set for standard examinations, not all.

b275.keyPoint: Fluoroscopy entrance surface dose is a rate, typically of the order of 10-50 mGy per minute.

b276.keyPoint: IRMER covers medico-legal exposures, stochastic effects are assumed to have no threshold, and childhood cancer risk is about 1 in 13,000 per mSv.

b277.keyPoint: The dose limit for the lens of the eye is expressed as an equivalent dose because the lens is a radiosensitive tissue prone to cataract.

b278.keyPoint: ARSAC authority is site- and practice-specific, paediatric activity is scaled by weight, and pregnancy is not an absolute contraindication to nuclear medicine.

b279.keyPoint: kVp is checked with a calibrated meter (a step wedge tests contrast response), and image intensifiers - not the whole unit - are distorted by magnetic fields.

b280.keyPoint: X-ray tube output is QA-tested every one to two months with an ionisation chamber, not merely annually.

b281.keyPoint: An X-ray photon may pass through unaffected, be completely absorbed, or scatter with energy loss - it never gains energy, and backscatter loses the most.

b282.keyPoint: Effective focal spot size depends on the actual focal spot and target angle - not anode disc diameter, target material or anode-cathode distance.

b283.keyPoint: Increasing the target angle increases effective focal spot size; target material has no effect on it.

b284.keyPoint: Compton scatter predominates at CT energies, fat is about -100 HU, and subpixel objects can still be visible through partial volume averaging.

b285.keyPoint: Ideal diagnostic radionuclides emit gamma photons of roughly 100-250 keV with a short practical half-life; several (F-18, I-123) are cyclotron-produced.

b286.keyPoint: The pulse height analyser rejects scattered events to cut noise, while crystal thickness and collimator hole geometry set the resolution-sensitivity trade-off.

b287.keyPoint: Tissue heating in ultrasound is mainly from absorption of acoustic energy; probe surface heating reflects internal transducer losses and poor coupling.

b288.keyPoint: Posterior enhancement behind fluid is a propagation (low attenuation) effect, not TGC; pulse-echo systems spend about 99% of each cycle receiving.

b289.keyPoint: The operator controls PRF, focal zone position and (indirectly through depth, sector width and line density) frame rate.

b290.keyPoint: The MR controlled area begins at the 0.5 mT (5 gauss) contour, with an inner controlled area at 3 mT overseen by the MR Responsible Person.

b291.keyPoint: Normal-mode SAR limits keep whole-body temperature rise to about 1 degree Celsius, and first-trimester pregnancy is not an absolute MRI contraindication.

b292.keyPoint: Gradient echo uses a bipolar readout gradient, small flip angles and short TR, giving fast low-SAR imaging without a 180 degree pulse.

b293.keyPoint: Chemical shift artefact (from the 3.5 ppm fat-water difference) lies along the frequency-encoding axis, grows with B0, and shrinks with wider bandwidth.

b294.keyPoint: The K-shell holds only 2 electrons, K-shell binding energy rises with atomic (not mass) number, and outermost-shell electrons determine chemical properties.

b295.keyPoint: Photoelectric absorption occurs in K, L or M shells, produces characteristic radiation, and its strong Z-dependence creates subject contrast; mA does not change its probability.

b296.keyPoint: In Compton scatter the electron receives more energy at wider scatter angles, and Compton dominates soft tissue at nuclear medicine photon energies.

b297.keyPoint: The effective focal spot is the projected (smaller) version of the real focal spot, set by filament size and target angle - typically 0.6 mm fine and 1.2 mm broad.

b298.keyPoint: Raising kVp from 60 to 80 nearly doubles output (intensity proportional to kVp squared), cutting mAs and entrance dose but reducing photoelectric interactions and contrast.

b299.keyPoint: A CR plate is a continuous phosphor sensitive to any ionising radiation; phosphor thickness is limited by readout laser light spread, and underexposure raises noise.

b300.keyPoint: Brightness gain equals flux gain times minification gain (typically 5000-10000); minification gain uses screen areas, edge darkening is vignetting, and magnification mode improves resolution at higher dose.

b301.keyPoint: Tc-99m decays by isomeric transition emitting a 140 keV gamma with no beta; the NaI crystal absorbs about 90%, and effective half-life depends on the radiopharmaceutical.

b302.keyPoint: Nuclear medicine image contrast depends on PHA window width, injection-to-scan delay and radiochemical purity - not on collimator type or patient-collimator distance.

b303.keyPoint: Bone scan resolution is about 10 mm FWHM worsening with collimator distance; 600 MBq is the DRL (not a legal limit) and effective dose about 3 mSv.

b304.keyPoint: SPECT needs higher administered activity and high-resolution collimators, and is degraded by attenuation, camera non-uniformity and poorer resolution than planar imaging.

b305.keyPoint: PET uses dense scintillators (BGO, LSO, GSO - not NaI), coincidence detection of two 511 keV photons, higher sensitivity than SPECT, and best resolution at ring centre.

b306.keyPoint: Cancer induction is stochastic, lens opacity is deterministic with a threshold near 0.5 Gy (2 Gy causes point opacities), and X- and gamma rays share a weighting factor of 1.

b307.keyPoint: A controlled area is designated where annual effective dose may exceed 6 mSv, needs warning signs, local rules and an RPS - pregnant staff may still enter.

b308.keyPoint: DRLs are typical doses for standard-sized patients in any convenient dose quantity, reviewable annually, achievable nationally, and exceedable in justified individual cases.

b309.keyPoint: Each administered activity must be measured beforehand under IRMER; ARSAC publishes national DRLs, routes include oral and inhaled, and about 40% of Tc-99m is excreted as liquid waste.

b310.keyPoint: The bow-tie filter controls peripheral dose, beam hardening occurs at bone-soft tissue junctions, and CT numbers vary with kVp but not with mA.

b311.keyPoint: CT resolution improves with smaller focal spots, smaller detectors and shorter scan times; interpolation to a bigger matrix and thicker slices do not help.

b312.keyPoint: CT noise rises with larger matrix (smaller pixels) and obese patients, and falls with higher mA or slower rotation; window width only changes noise visibility.

b313.keyPoint: CTDI is measured in mGy in Perspex phantoms (16 cm head, 32 cm body - head values higher), is proportional to mA, and CTDIvol falls as pitch rises.

b314.keyPoint: CT patient dose is proportional to mAs, falls with faster rotation and higher pitch, can be cut by iterative reconstruction, and abdomen-pelvis studies give about 8 mSv.

b315.keyPoint: The Larmor precession frequency is proportional to field strength and the gyromagnetic ratio, and is unaffected by relaxation times.

b316.keyPoint: M0 is the net spin-population vector proportional to B0; a 90 degree pulse tips it fully transverse, a 180 degree pulse inverts it, and rotating transverse magnetisation induces the signal.

b317.keyPoint: In spin echo the 180 degree pulse refocuses dephasing so the echo appears at TE after the 90 degree pulse; TR and TE choices set T1 or T2 weighting.

b318.keyPoint: GRE uses sub-90 flip angles and a bipolar gradient (no 180 pulse), yields T2*-weighted images sensitive to field inhomogeneity, and suits MR angiography.

b319.keyPoint: Ultrasound travels at 1540 m/s in soft tissue and about 4000 m/s in bone, is non-ionising, deposits energy in collagen-rich tissue, and has 0.3-1 mm wavelengths.

b320.keyPoint: Ultrasound attenuates exponentially (about 0.5-1 dB/cm/MHz in soft tissue), mostly ending as heat, with reflection and refraction at impedance boundaries and scattering by subwavelength structures.

b321.keyPoint: Axial resolution equals half the spatial pulse length and is independent of depth; transducer diameter and focusing affect lateral resolution instead.

b322.keyPoint: Reflected frequency rises for approaching targets, the shift is greatest parallel to flow, pulsed Doppler is limited to half the PRF, and continuous wave Doppler never aliases.

b323.keyPoint: Ultrasound heating is greatest in bone, foetal scan time is restricted above TI 0.7, neonatal lung damage can occur above MI 0.3, and microbubbles promote cavitation.

b324.keyPoint: Photon energy is proportional to frequency (expressed in eV), all photons travel at light speed, and X-rays and gamma rays of equal energy are identical apart from origin.

b325.keyPoint: Photoelectric absorption needs photon energy above the binding energy and dominates in iodine (Z=53, probability about Z cubed), while Compton dominates soft tissue at CT energies.

b326.keyPoint: Bremsstrahlung (about 1% efficient at diagnostic energies) rises with kVp and target Z; K-characteristic X-ray energy sits just below the K-shell binding energy.

b327.keyPoint: Radiographic spatial resolution improves with a smaller focal spot and shorter patient-receptor distance; mA, grid ratio and filtration do not change it.

b328.keyPoint: Higher kVp raises HVL and ESD (with kVp squared), cuts quantum mottle, and lowers effective dose when receptor dose is held constant.

b329.keyPoint: Only pixel size (not bit depth) sets digital spatial resolution; subpixel objects remain visible via partial volume, and a 10,000:1 dynamic range cuts repeat exposures.

b330.keyPoint: In DSA the mask is subtracted from the live image using logarithmic subtraction, which removes overlying tissue but increases noise and leaves resolution unchanged.

b331.keyPoint: Mammography uses 25-35 kVp, a 0.3 mm focal spot and about 65 cm SID; K-edge filtration keeps the useful characteristic X-rays in the beam.

b332.keyPoint: Tc-99m is eluted daily from the Mo-99 generator; its 140 keV gammas have about 5 cm soft-tissue HVL and interact mainly by Compton scattering.

b333.keyPoint: Longer acquisitions cut noise, thyroid Tc-99m DRL is 80 MBq, and high-resolution collimators need longer (not shorter) acquisition times due to lower sensitivity.

b334.keyPoint: PET resolution (about 4 mm) beats SPECT (about 10 mm); finer angular sampling improves SPECT, and PET bed positions overlap about 33% for axial sensitivity.

b335.keyPoint: Adult FDG PET/CT injects 250-350 MBq (about 6 mSv, exceeding the CT component), uses a 60-minute uptake, and must correct random coincidences.

b336.keyPoint: IRR17 requires HSE registration, ALARP optimisation and employer-led protection (the RPA only advises); medical exposures have no dose limits.

b337.keyPoint: Under IRMER anyone performing QC on medical radiation equipment is an operator, each duty holder answers for their own role, and nuclear medicine needs both practitioner and employer licences.

b338.keyPoint: About 40% of administered Tc-99m enters the sewer via urine (discharged directly, not delayed), solid Tc-99m waste decays on-site for a week, and the RWA oversees permit compliance.

b339.keyPoint: UK average annual dose is about 2.7 mSv (15% medical); 10 mSv carries about 1 in 2000 cancer risk, and 25 mSv in utero roughly doubles childhood cancer risk.

b340.keyPoint: Effective dose (in mSv) is the sum of organ equivalent doses times tissue weighting factors, quantifying stochastic risk only - not foetal dose or deterministic risk.

b341.keyPoint: In MDCT, pre-patient collimation defines the irradiated volume (a detector grid removes scatter), the bow-tie filter modulates dose, and contrast largely reflects tissue density.

b342.keyPoint: CT SNR scales with the square root of mAs, falls with higher pitch, is altered by the reconstruction filter, and is unaffected by display window width.

b343.keyPoint: CT effective dose is unaffected by pixel size or reconstructed slice thickness, rises with scan length, and is about 1-2 mSv for a routine brain scan.

b344.keyPoint: Adult thorax-abdomen-pelvis CT uses spiral acquisition at 120 kVp or more with about 0.7 lp/mm resolution; contrast injection precedes scanning by a timed delay.

b345.keyPoint: The MR signal is a voltage induced by rotating transverse magnetisation of hydrogen nuclei, grows with B0, decays by T2 relaxation, and follows no signal after a lone 180 pulse.

b346.keyPoint: T1 (typically 200-2000 ms) always exceeds T2, lengthens with field strength, and governs TR choice; T2 measures how fast the signal decays.

b347.keyPoint: MR spatial resolution improves with thinner slices, larger matrix and smaller FOV - higher B0 or TE change SNR, not resolution.

b348.keyPoint: Chemical shift artefact stems from intrinsic fat-water Larmor frequency differences (not field inhomogeneity), lies along frequency encoding, worsens at high field, and is minimised by STIR.

b349.keyPoint: Only ferromagnetic objects are projectile hazards, rapid gradient switching causes peripheral nerve stimulation, and SAR quantifies RF tissue heating.

b350.keyPoint: Acoustic impedance (in Rayls) rises with tissue density and sound speed, is motion-independent, and is higher in muscle than fat.

b351.keyPoint: B-mode sends one pulse per scan line in real time, PRF is limited by imaging depth, and brightness reflects impedance differences at interfaces, strongest at normal incidence.

b352.keyPoint: Axial resolution equals half the spatial pulse length (typically 0.5-1 mm), improves with frequency, and is independent of depth and transducer diameter.

b353.keyPoint: Doppler shift rises with operating frequency and blood velocity, falls as the angle approaches 90 degrees, and is inversely proportional to propagation velocity - PRF only sets the aliasing limit.

b354.keyPoint: Binding energy is the energy to remove an electron from the atom, greatest for K-shell (typically 10-70 keV), rising with atomic number, and gating photoelectric events.

b355.keyPoint: Photoelectrons travel under 2 mm in tissue, Compton (incoherent) scatter dominates above 100 keV with increasingly forward-directed scatter, and elastic scatter deposits no dose.

b356.keyPoint: Added filtration removes low-energy bremsstrahlung without changing maximum energy; inherent filtration is about 0.5 mm Al, and more filtration raises HVL.

b357.keyPoint: A larger matrix improves sampling, more photons per pixel raise SNR, low-pass filtering suppresses noise, and subvoxel high-contrast structures remain detectable.

b358.keyPoint: In flat panels a photoconductor makes charge directly while a phosphor makes light (screen blur limits indirect FPD resolution); dynamic range is about 10,000:1 and FPDs serve fluoroscopy.

b359.keyPoint: Fluoroscopy quantum noise falls with higher kVp or mA, grid removal, or an alternative ABC dose curve - anything that increases detected photons.

b360.keyPoint: X-ray contrast improves by lowering kVp, collimating the beam and using a grid - all reduce scatter or boost photoelectric interactions; mA has no effect.

b361.keyPoint: Electron capture and positron emission both occur in proton-rich nuclei and lower Z by one; isomeric transition (Tc-99m) emits gamma without changing atomic number.

b362.keyPoint: The collimator forms the image (the PHA window rejects scatter by energy), NaI converts gammas to light, and faulty PM tubes cause circular uniformity defects.

b363.keyPoint: Higher administered activity raises SNR without changing scatter fraction, parallel-hole collimators keep 1:1 magnification, and impurities alter biodistribution and contrast.

b364.keyPoint: F-18 positrons span energies up to 635 keV with short range, PET rings are stationary, resolution peaks centrally, and random coincidences fog contrast.

b365.keyPoint: SUV equals tissue FDG concentration divided by injected activity per body mass, and varies with scanner, uptake time and reconstruction algorithm.

b366.keyPoint: IRR17 limits sit below tissue-reaction thresholds and none may be exceeded: 20 mSv for the lens, 150 mSv extremities (forcing classification), and 1 mSv to the foetus, not the mother.

b367.keyPoint: IRMER covers screening and research, any entitled trained registered professional can be a practitioner, optimisation means the lowest dose giving diagnostic information, and duty holders can be prosecuted individually.

b368.keyPoint: 6 mSv, typical of a chest CT, carries about 1 in 3000 cancer risk and is the three-tenths threshold for classifying staff.

b369.keyPoint: Scatter at 1 m is about 0.1% of the incident dose rate, tube leakage must stay under 1 mGy/h at 1 m, and lead aprons stop only scatter.

b370.keyPoint: CT numbers vary with kVp, slice thickness (partial volume), surrounding anatomy (beam hardening) and reconstruction algorithm - but not with mA.

b371.keyPoint: Raising pitch from 1.0 to 1.5 cuts dose, scan time and motion artefact, but increases noise and partial volume effects.

b372.keyPoint: FBP is faster with sharper detail; iterative reconstruction suppresses noise and metal/beam-hardening artefacts better, and both suffer motion artefacts equally.

b373.keyPoint: CT noise falls with slower gantry rotation and smaller matrix (larger pixels), but rises when slice thickness, kVp or mA are decreased.

b374.keyPoint: Metal causes streaks, faulty detectors cause rings (not motion), beam hardening causes cupping, and zebra artefacts arise from helical interpolation.

b375.keyPoint: Excitation frequency (Larmor) is proportional to B0, gradients define the imaged slice, fat and water precess at slightly different frequencies, and gadolinium shortens T1 more than T2.

b376.keyPoint: Slice thickness depends on RF pulse bandwidth and gradient slope, frequency encoding is applied during readout, and acquisition time is proportional to phase-encode matrix size.

b377.keyPoint: MRI SNR rises with thicker slices and larger FOV, and falls with longer TE and wider receiver bandwidth; extra phase-encoding steps add resolution, not SNR.

b378.keyPoint: MR scanners have three gradient coil sets, cryogen-cooled superconducting magnets (quenching destroys the field), a transmit-receive RF coil, and a fringe field extending metres.

b379.keyPoint: The transducer listens over 99% of the time, TGC amplifies deep echoes to offset attenuation, and refraction occurs at oblique boundaries with different sound speeds.

b380.keyPoint: Lateral resolution (typically 2-3 mm, worse than axial) improves with frequency and line density, varies with depth, and trades off against frame rate.

b381.keyPoint: TGC compensates for depth-dependent attenuation so similar boundaries give similar signals - it does not affect axial resolution and narrows the displayed dynamic range.

b382.keyPoint: Speed errors displace structures axially, reverberation causes comet tails, side lobes misplace off-axis echoes, and cysts cause enhancement, not shadowing.

b383.keyPoint: Ultrasound heating rises with PRF and frequency, peaks superficially and in bone, and is reduced in well-perfused tissue where blood carries heat away.

b384.keyPoint: Photoelectric absorption dominates at mammographic energies (about 20 keV), completely absorbs the photon, and falls with 1/E cubed while rising with density and atomic number.

b385.keyPoint: Compton scatter involves outer-shell electrons, slowly decreases with kVp, always degrades contrast, and dominates in patients at CT energies - but not in high-Z CsI detectors.

b386.keyPoint: The linear attenuation coefficient is the fractional intensity loss per unit thickness, equals 0.693/HVL, is energy- (not mAs-) dependent, and is higher for bone than water.

b387.keyPoint: Scatter is reduced by collimation, compression, lower kVp and an air gap - increasing mA changes quantity but not the scatter fraction.

b388.keyPoint: Sharpness improves with longer focus-to-patient distance and smaller focal spot; grids, kVp and a larger patient-receptor gap do not help.

b389.keyPoint: CR resolution is typically 4 lp/mm, limited by laser spot size and plate size; fading is gradual (15-20 minute delays tolerable) and contrast is set by post-processing.

b390.keyPoint: Image intensifiers use a CsI input phosphor with output light driving automatic exposure control; abdominal surface dose rates run 10-20 mGy/min and brightness gain falls with age.

b391.keyPoint: Mammography uses a 65 cm focus-receptor distance, K-edge filtration and long exposures; compression improves contrast and sharpness, while magnification increases quantum mottle.

b392.keyPoint: The ideal gamma-camera radionuclide has a 4-6 hour half-life, 100-200 keV gamma emission, a stable daughter, and generator (not cyclotron) availability.

b393.keyPoint: NaI detects about 90% of 140 keV gammas, the collimator dominates resolution, dead time breaks count-rate linearity at high activity, and under 0.1% of emitted gammas form the image.

b394.keyPoint: SPECT acquires up to 120 projections at about 3 degree steps, uses patient-contoured orbits and iterative reconstruction, and corrects attenuation (not camera non-uniformity) with CT.

b395.keyPoint: PET axial FOV is 15-25 cm requiring bed positions, CT is acquired first, time-of-flight needs fast (non-BGO) scintillators, and generator-produced Rb-82 and Ga-68 have higher Z.

b396.keyPoint: IRR17 requires critical examination at installation, dose investigation levels in local rules, 30-year classified dose records, and limits the foetal (not maternal) dose to 1 mSv.

b397.keyPoint: The employer reports significant accidental exposures to the CQC within 2 weeks; reporting thresholds scale with intended dose, and equipment-fault overexposures are reportable.

b398.keyPoint: Absorbed dose is energy per unit mass; in diagnostic radiology equivalent dose equals absorbed dose (weighting factor 1), and effective dose compares stochastic risk across examinations.

b399.keyPoint: Radiopharmaceutical dose depends on both radionuclide and pharmaceutical, is delivered at a far lower dose rate than CT, and limits image quality via administered activity.

b400.keyPoint: All activities are measured in a dose calibrator first; paediatric doses scale by weight, operators can authorise under protocol, and breastfeeding interruption is radiopharmaceutical-specific.

b401.keyPoint: CT beams are heavily pre-hardened with copper or tin, detectors are gadolinium oxysulphide scintillators, the tube runs continuously, and pitch divides table travel by collimated beam width.

b402.keyPoint: CT noise increases with thinner slices, lower kVp and sharp (bone) reconstruction filters; slower rotation and smaller matrices reduce it.

b403.keyPoint: In MSCT detector element size sets slice thickness, quarter-detector offset boosts transaxial sampling, ring artefacts still occur helically, and CT numbers are relative to water.

b404.keyPoint: Effective dose is proportional to DLP via conversion factors; chest-abdomen-pelvis CT gives 12-15 mSv, pelvic CT delivers 20-30 mGy to a foetus, and DRLs are guidance, not limits.

b405.keyPoint: T1 (spin-lattice) is the 63% recovery time and lengthens with B0; T2 (30-100 ms) reflects random spin-spin interactions - inhomogeneity effects belong to T2*.

b406.keyPoint: Fat and water protons precess at different frequencies, STIR (short TI) nulls fat while CSF nulling needs long TI, and inflowing blood is dark on spin echo.

b407.keyPoint: MR SNR is proportional to proton density and higher in T1-weighted (short TE) images; wider receiver bandwidth admits more noise and quadrupling matrix size quarters voxel signal.

b408.keyPoint: Motion (not field inhomogeneity) causes phase-axis ghosting, GRE shows worse metal signal voids than SE, and wraparound is cured by enlarging the FOV.

b409.keyPoint: The Faraday cage blocks RF (not fringe field), public access is allowed below 0.5 mT, only ferromagnetic items are projectiles, and gadolinium in later pregnancy raises stillbirth risk.

b410.keyPoint: Soft-tissue attenuation is about 0.5-1 dB/cm/MHz, exponential with depth, mainly due to absorption, frequency-dependent, and unrelated to acoustic impedance.

b411.keyPoint: Crystal thickness (not diameter) sets resonant frequency, spatial pulse length shrinks with frequency, reflections under 1% are detectable, and sound is faster in muscle than fat.

b412.keyPoint: Phased arrays steer and focus scan lines, linear arrays give rectangular fields, harmonic imaging receives at twice the transmitted frequency, and speckle arises from subwavelength scattering interference.

b413.keyPoint: Higher frequency improves resolution but increases attenuation, heating risk and Doppler aliasing, while wave speed stays fixed by the medium.

b414.keyPoint: General X-ray equipment needs at least 2.5 mm Al equivalent total filtration (inherent about 0.5-1 mm); CT is filtered more heavily and 0.1-0.5 mm copper can be added.

b415.keyPoint: X-ray photon quantity rises with kVp (approximately kVp squared), target atomic number and reduced filtration - anode-cathode distance is irrelevant.

b416.keyPoint: 1 MBq is one million disintegrations per second, half-life equals 0.693 divided by the decay constant, and physical half-life is independent of biological clearance.

b417.keyPoint: Beam quality depends on peak kV, voltage waveform, anode atomic number and angle, and tube window material.

b418.keyPoint: QA uses ionisation chambers for leakage and output, HVL measurement to estimate total filtration, and accepts about 2 lp/mm for fluoroscopy systems.

b419.keyPoint: MRI SNR increases with shorter TE, larger FOV, higher field strength and thicker slices; a larger matrix reduces it.

b420.keyPoint: Compton (energy shared between electron and scattered photon) dominates in CT, forward scatter grows with energy, and pair production yields 1.02 MeV of annihilation radiation.

b421.keyPoint: Useful dose benchmarks: barium enema about 7 mSv, chest X-ray ESD about 150 uGy, 100 MBq Tc-99m lung perfusion about 1 mSv, UK medical average about 400 uSv per year.

b422.keyPoint: The Nyquist limit (half the PRF) caps measurable velocity, power Doppler shows amplitude but not direction, and thicker crystals emit longer wavelengths.

b423.keyPoint: Classification is required when a worker is likely to exceed 6 mSv effective dose or three-tenths of any dose limit - pregnancy or multiple sites do not trigger it.

b424.keyPoint: CR plates are read by a red laser and erased with bright white light; CR has wide dynamic range but is less dose-efficient than DR.

b425.keyPoint: CT is a high-dose modality with about 10 lp/cm resolution on a 512x512 matrix; narrow window widths display subtle density differences.

b426.keyPoint: Gyromagnetic ratios differ between nuclei, Larmor frequency rises with B0, and water protons precess about 3.5 ppm faster than fat protons.

b427.keyPoint: Interventional skin dose falls with greater tube-to-patient distance, beam angulation and varied projections; increasing patient-to-detector distance raises it.

b428.keyPoint: Annual limits: public 1 mSv, classified workers 20 mSv effective and 500 mSv skin; UK natural background averages about 2.7 mSv.

b429.keyPoint: Photoelectric absorption involves inner-shell electrons, totally absorbs the photon and ionises the atom, falling with energy and rising with Z cubed.

b430.keyPoint: Each CT pixel represents the voxel's average linear attenuation coefficient (dependent on density and composition); fat is about -100 HU and bone windows use high levels.

b431.keyPoint: Iodinated contrast works by photoelectric absorption with a K-edge at about 33 keV, and positive plus negative agents can be combined for double-contrast studies.

b432.keyPoint: The ideal geometry minimises focal spot and object-detector distance while maximising focus-detector distance; mammographic magnification deliberately raises object-detector distance.

b433.keyPoint: Most radiation damage is indirect via free radicals; LET is energy per unit path length, alpha particles have high LET, and RBE compares doses for equal biological effect.

b434.keyPoint: Any entitled professional can be an IRMER practitioner (one person may hold all three roles); the employer bears overall compliance responsibility and optimisation means ALARP, not best image.

b435.keyPoint: Gamma photons are nuclear emissions with wave-particle duality, can ionise atoms, may be emitted without changing atomic or mass number, and outpenetrate alpha and beta.

b436.keyPoint: Point-source intensity follows the inverse square law (doubling distance quarters intensity), which does not account for attenuation in materials such as lead.

b437.keyPoint: Patient scatter is the main staff exposure, entrance surface dose varies with kV squared, and in-utero childhood cancer risk is about 1 in 13,000 per mGy.

b438.keyPoint: Fast flow gives spin echo flow voids but is bright on GRE; ghosts appear along phase encoding, and truncation ringing is reduced by increasing the matrix.

b439.keyPoint: Mammography dose is quoted as mean glandular dose in mGy - below about 2.5 mGy per image for a standard NHSBSP breast - because glandular tissue is the radiosensitive target.

b440.keyPoint: Inversion recovery starts with a 180 degree pulse and long TR; STIR (short TI) suppresses fat while FLAIR (long TI) nulls CSF.

b441.keyPoint: PET detects 511 keV photons from short-lived positron emitters using ring detectors, with coincidence detection replacing lead collimators; it is not low dose.

b442.keyPoint: Thermionic emission happens at the cathode filament; bremsstrahlung and characteristic X-rays form at the anode, with only about 1% of electron energy becoming X-rays.

b443.keyPoint: National DRLs exist for common examinations (as administered activity in nuclear medicine) and employers must audit local DRLs; exceeding one triggers review, not automatic reporting.

b444.keyPoint: Scatter mainly degrades contrast, increases with kV, and is reduced by grids - which improve contrast but raise patient dose.

b445.keyPoint: Quantum noise dominates CT and limits low-contrast detectability; SNR improves with higher mA, longer rotation or higher kV, and falls with thinner slices.

b446.keyPoint: Element timing focuses and steers array beams (annular arrays cannot steer), curvilinear arrays give sector fields, narrower sectors raise frame rate, and matching layers aid coupling.

b447.keyPoint: CT filtration exceeds 2.5 mm Al, bow-tie filters offset the patient's elliptical shape, and post-patient collimation rejects scatter; collimation width is millimetres to centimetres.

b448.keyPoint: DSA patient dose is cut with 0.2 mm copper filtration and monitored by DAP meter; faster frame rates increase, not decrease, dose.

b449.keyPoint: Pulse-echo imaging assumes similar soft-tissue sound speeds, uses pulsed emission and narrow beams for localisation, with TGC manually offsetting depth attenuation.

b450.keyPoint: The 90 degree pulse creates transverse magnetisation, the 180 degree refocusing pulse fires at TE/2, and the echo forms at TE - TR is the interval between excitations.

b451.keyPoint: Tc-99m emits 140 keV, F-18 is cyclotron- (not generator-) produced, gamma cameras use NaI (BGO is PET), and wider collimator holes raise sensitivity, not lower dose.

b452.keyPoint: Under AEC, patient dose falls with faster detectors and smaller field sizes; grids raise it, and lowering mA just lengthens exposure time.

b453.keyPoint: Magnification rises with shorter focus-receptor or longer object-receptor distance and is independent of focal spot size, which instead governs unsharpness.
